hypothesis: Once claim input is held constant across configurations (baselines given TruthLens's own extracted claims instead of items.jsonl's hand-written claim summary), does the accuracy comparison between full TruthLens and Baselines 1-3 change?
baseline: Original (superseded) paired comparison: B1 0.0%, B2 66.7%, B3 50.0%, TruthLens 33.3%
variant: Baselines re-run one call per real extracted claim, aggregated via derive_overall_verdict()
confidence_interval: Wilson 95% per cell, reported in main.tex Table IV
failure_cases: items 0006/0007 (zero verifiable claims extracted for either baseline or TruthLens); item-0004 (TruthLens validator false negative)
interpretation: Reversed the program's headline finding: TruthLens now beats 2 of 3 baselines outright and trails Baseline 2 by 16.7 points instead of 33.4. The prior negative result was substantially an artifact of unequal claim input, not a property of the architecture.

hypothesis: Do two general, ground-truth-independent validator fixes (UUID-leak stripping; new reasoning/label-consistency check) improve validator recall against human-judged unsupported output, without reducing precision, on the same 9-claim audit sample?
variant: validate_verdict() with both general fixes applied, re-scored on the same 9 cases, no new LLM calls
model: n/a (re-scoring is deterministic, not a model call)
validator_version: 5 checks (added reasoning/label-consistency check to the prior 4)
result: precision 100% (2/2), recall 40% (2/5); reel-level accuracy unchanged at 2/6, both before and after
failure_cases: n/a (this experiment measures an improvement, not a residual failure set)
interpretation: Validator recall improved while reel-level (label) accuracy stayed exactly the same -- concrete evidence that label accuracy and support validity (whether a verdict's own citations/numbers/reasoning hold up) are separable, independently-moving properties of this system.

hypothesis: Does aggregating all extracted claims (vs. only the single highest-importance claim) improve reel-level verdict accuracy on items with more than one verifiable claim?
model: n/a (counterfactual reanalysis of already-collected verdicts, no new LLM calls)
confidence_interval: none computed -- n=4 too small for an informative CI, raw counts reported instead
failure_cases: item-0004 (single-claim item, aggregation is a no-op, still wrong); item-0005 (wrong under both conditions)
interpretation: The clearest component-level evidence in this program that the aggregation mechanism specifically helps once claim extraction has more than one claim to work with. Explicitly relabeled a 'counterfactual reanalysis,' not an 'ablation' -- it isolates the aggregation mechanism only, not the upstream decision to decompose.

hypothesis: Does adding more input modalities (OCR, then vision-context) to claim extraction improve claim-coverage recall against professional fact-checkers' own claims, relative to transcript-only extraction?
dataset: 6 of 7 successfully-ingested benchmark items (item-0003 excluded, never ingested)
model: llama3.2 (Ollama), local-only, no Gemini fallback (isolates the modality variable)
metrics: claim-coverage recall (human-judged, blind to which condition produced the extraction)
confidence_interval: Wilson 95% per condition, reported in main.tex Table XI
failure_cases: text_ocr scoring below text_only on this sample -- reported as real, not suppressed; likely single-call noise compounded by a specific extraction failure, not a robust modality effect at this n
interpretation: Full multimodal extraction recovers claims the other two conditions miss (item-0004's on-screen figure, invisible to audio-only). n=6, single non-repeated call per condition -- directional only.

hypothesis: Does a deterministic entity-consistency check (does a claim's extracted entity appear in its cited evidence text?) catch real errors on the actual 9-claim benchmark sample at a rate justifying its integration as a 5th validator check?
dataset: 9-claim validator audit sample, 10 non-irrelevant evidence rows
baseline: n/a (new capability, not an improvement to an existing check)
variant: prototype entity-consistency check (backend/research/entity_consistency_eval.py), not integrated into production
validator_version: prototype only, never added to validate_verdict()
metrics: manual-audit precision (true positive vs. false positive rate among flagged rows)
result: 7/9 evaluable rows flagged; 1 genuine true positive (Delhi Police claim vs. Burdwan, West Bengal evidence), 4 false positives (abstract-concept entities like 'Democracy'), 1-2 likely false positives (transliteration variance), 1 structurally unevaluable case
confidence_interval: none -- manual audit of every flagged case at this n, not a formula
failure_cases: see result -- the 4+1 false-positive cases are the failure set
interpretation: One real catch is a genuine, useful finding (refined item-0004's error attribution), but too small a sample to justify a 5th deterministic check without more data, per the governing protocol's own complexity-needs-justification rule. Not integrated; reported as an honest, mixed result.

hypothesis: Does the new reasoning/label-consistency check (Check 4) generalize to real paraphrases of 'no evidence found' reasoning it was not calibrated on, and how do all 4 deterministic validator checks perform on a broader set of synthetic adversarial cases?
dataset: 28 hand-constructed synthetic VerdictProposal cases run through the real validate_verdict()
split: dev/test (14/14, tracked in the artifact's own split field)
baseline: n/a (first evaluation of the validator on synthetic adversarial cases)
model: n/a (synthetic cases, real deterministic validator, no LLM calls)
metrics: precision, recall, F1, specificity; per-category catch rate
result: TP=9, FP=2, FN=9, TN=8; precision 81.8% (9/11), recall 50.0% (9/18), specificity 80.0% (8/10), F1 62.1%. All 4 novel paraphrase test cases (categories K/L/M/N) were missed.
confidence_interval: none reported -- categorical pass/fail counts at this n, not treated as an estimate of a population rate
failure_cases: categories K/L/M/N (4 real paraphrases never in Check 4's original phrase list, e.g. 'the data does not corroborate this'); category O (citation exists/topically related but doesn't entail the specific claim)
interpretation: The 'checkable_by_current_checks' design label perfectly predicted real behavior in all 18 positive cases (9/9 within-design caught, 0/9 outside-design caught) -- directly resolved a previously-open question: Check 4 does NOT generalize beyond its literal phrase list.

hypothesis: Does restricting research-planning queries explicitly targeting primary sources to a fixed government/legal domain allow-list (instead of a free-text site:gov.in the model writes itself) improve the source-tier classification rate?
dataset: 7 real, unscripted domain-restricted queries (distinct, smaller sample than the main evidence-quality run)
baseline: ~11% (8/72) tier classification under normal, unrestricted queries
variant: domain-restricted queries + a related source-classifier fix (missing NIC-/RBI-hosted domain patterns)
result: 95% (19/20) landed in a primary tier, of 4 queries that returned results (pooling to 20 sources)
confidence_interval: percentages only, both from real counts
failure_cases: domain restriction guarantees tier correctness, not topical relevance -- one query returned five correctly-tiered but topically irrelevant results; one query's five URLs all failed full-page fetch (403s/TLS errors), falling back to snippet text
interpretation: A real, large improvement in tier classification, on a distinct (smaller) sample from the main n=68 evidence-quality run -- not directly comparable to it, disclosed as such.

hypothesis: Is TruthLens's apparent evidence-quality bottleneck actually poor retrieval relevance, or is retrieval finding real, on-topic sources that are simply too generic to confirm one specific atomic fact?
dataset: 68 sources across 9 claims from the validator audit sample
baseline: n/a (first four-way decomposition of this metric)
model: n/a (draft human judgment for relevance; deterministic counts for the other 3 metrics)
metrics: source-tier classification rate; relevant-primary-source rate; primary-source fetch-success rate; usable-evidence extraction rate
result: tier classification 23.5% (16/68); relevance among primary-tier sources 68.75% (11/16); fetch-success 16/16 (by construction); usable-evidence extraction 18.75% (3/16)
confidence_interval: Wilson 95% on metric 1 only (15.0-34.9%); others reported as exact counts at this n
failure_cases: the 5 primary-tier sources judged not relevant (a wrong-domain case: engineering-admissions authority for a medical/NEET claim; a wrong-country case: US National Archives for an Indian claim)
interpretation: The gap between metric 2 (68.75%) and metric 4 (18.75%) is the single most important finding of this evaluation: retrieval finds real, topically-appropriate primary sources at a meaningfully higher rate than the usable-evidence number alone would suggest -- the bottleneck is source specificity (most are homepages/generic documents too broad to confirm one atomic fact), not a failure to find relevant sources.

hypothesis: Does an explicit recall-first instruction in the claim-extraction prompt (claim_extraction.v4-recall-candidate) increase claim recall relative to the current production prompt (claim_extraction.v3), without increasing raw schema-validation failure rate, when both are run via the same local model with no Gemini fallback?
dataset: 5 real reels already in the dev database: 3 with real, non-garbled signal (items 0001/0002/0004) and 2 deliberately included as a negative control (items 0006/0007, known garbled/degraded transcripts)
variant: claim_extraction.v4-recall-candidate (explicit recall-first instruction + lower-confidence guidance for borderline inclusions)
model: llama3.2 (Ollama), direct OllamaProvider calls only -- no Gemini fallback, isolating the prompt variable the same way baseline isolation does elsewhere in this program
metrics: claim count; verifiable count; raw schema-validation failure rate per condition
result: Of 10 raw attempts (5 items x 2 conditions): 4 failed schema validation outright (v3: items 0001, 0006, 0007; v4: items 0002, 0006, 0007), 2 more produced only schema-valid-but-empty-text claims (v3 on items 0002 and 0004; v4 on item-0004) which production's existing empty-text filter would drop before persistence, and only 1 of 10 (v4 on item-0001) produced real, non-empty, schema-valid claims outright. v4 failed with 4 separate out-of-range values on item-0002 (importance -0.5 x3, 1.2 x1) where v3 had succeeded (with empty-text garbage); v3 failed on item-0001 from output truncation (EOF while parsing JSON at 12461 chars, likely a max_tokens=4096 shortfall), where v4 succeeded.
confidence_interval: none -- n=5 raw counts, not treated as a rate estimate
failure_cases: see result; full per-item detail in research/results/claim_extraction_recall_comparison_20260815.json
interpretation: No evidence the recall-first prompt improves reliability, and some evidence it may reduce structural stability on at least one real item (more claims attempted, more of them with wild out-of-range field values). The dominant real finding is NOT about the prompt at all: raw, single-model, no-fallback llama3.2 has a much higher real-world schema-failure/empty-output rate on real content than the smaller synthetic tests that originally calibrated this stage ever surfaced -- exactly why production's layered defenses (Gemini quality-retry escalation, empty-text filtering, the substantiveness checks) exist, and a concrete demonstration of how much reliability those layers are actually carrying. Also surfaced two new, real, disclosed findings during this run: a likely max_tokens-driven output-truncation failure mode, and a real float-boundary-noise value (-1.1111111111e-06) that fell just outside this pass's original clamp epsilon (fixed, see the commit widening it to 1e-4).

hypothesis: EXP-009 found raw, no-fallback Ollama failing schema validation on real content at a high rate. Does production's actual full extract_claims() stack -- quality-retry heuristic, Gemini escalation via the new centralized quota service, empty-text filtering, and this session's new deduplication -- actually recover on an item that failed raw?
dataset: item-0002 (https://www.instagram.com/reel/DbNU9W7xA9P/), the specific item where EXP-009's raw-Ollama-only v3 condition failed schema validation with 4 out-of-range field values
baseline: EXP-009's raw-provider-only result on the same item: schema validation failure, zero claims
variant: real extract_claims() call, full production stack, real GEMINI_API_KEY, run inside a transaction rolled back afterward so nothing was persisted to the live benchmark-tagged reel
metrics: did extraction succeed end-to-end; claim count and quality of the recovered output
result: Local llama3.2 failed identically to EXP-009 (this time extraction_confidence=-2, same class of out-of-range-value bug, confirming it's a real, reproducible local-model instability, not a one-off). FallbackLLMProvider correctly caught the ProviderError and escalated to Gemini through the new centralized quota service (app/services/ai/gemini_quota.py); Gemini succeeded, producing 3 real, substantive, correctly-classified claims in Hindi (2 factual/verifiable, 1 opinion/not-verifiable), each with a correctly-inferred source_modalities=['CAPTION'] (this session's new deterministic provenance inference), sensible importance/confidence values, and confidence_type=MODEL_CONFIDENCE set correctly. Verified via direct DB query that the rollback left zero residual claim or gemini_tasks rows.
confidence_interval: none -- single-item verification, not a rate estimate
failure_cases: none in this run -- this experiment specifically tested recovery, and recovery succeeded
interpretation: Production's existing Gemini-escalation safety net does recover from exactly the kind of raw-local-model failure EXP-009 surfaced, end-to-end, using the real centralized quota service built this session (not just the mock-based unit tests) for the first time against a real API call. This resolves EXP-009's main open question: the high raw failure rate EXP-009 measured is real, but production's layered defenses -- specifically the Gemini fallback -- are doing exactly the job they were built for, at least in this one real, verified case. Does not generalize past n=1; the two garbled-transcript items (0006/0007) were not re-tested here since their known root cause (transcription quality) is outside claim-extraction's own failure surface entirely.
artifact: backend/research/claim_extraction_v2/verify_production_safety_net.py (no persisted output artifact -- transaction rolled back by design)

hypothesis: Does this session's float-boundary-noise/confused-value clamp (app/schemas/claim.py, committed after EXP-009/010) change the multimodal claim-coverage picture (EXP-004/MULTIMODAL_EVALUATION.md) at all -- either by reducing raw schema-crash outcomes, or by recovering real claims on the two items (0006/0007) originally diagnosed as having zero verifiable claims due to genuinely garbled transcripts?
dataset: 9 already-ingested benchmark_v1 reels reused directly from the dev DB (item-0003 skipped, never ingested), 3 modality conditions each (text_only/text_ocr/text_ocr_vision), same run_condition()/MODALITY_CONDITIONS code as the original EXP-004 script, imported not reimplemented
baseline: EXP-004's original result (items 0001/0002/0004/0005/0006/0007 only, n=6, text_only 16.7%, text_ocr 0.0%, text_ocr_vision 33.3% claim-coverage) plus this session's own EXP-009/010 raw failure-rate observations
variant: same raw OllamaProvider calls, no Gemini fallback, but now parsed through ExtractedClaim with the confused-value clamp active
model: llama3.2 (Ollama), no Gemini fallback -- matches the original experiment's isolation design
metrics: schema-validation outcome (resolved vs. error) per attempt; raw claim count vs. non-empty (substantive) claim count per item/condition
result: 24/24 attempts resolved with zero schema-validation crashes (vs. EXP-009's same-item-pool baseline, which had 4 of 10 raw attempts crash outright). Of 54 raw claims returned across all conditions, only 23 (42.6%) had non-empty text -- the rest are the pre-existing, separately-diagnosed 'schema-valid, substantively empty output' failure mode (taxonomy #1), which the clamp does not and was not intended to address. Critically: items 0006 and 0007 (originally diagnosed as producing zero verifiable claims due to genuinely garbled transcripts) STILL produced zero non-empty claims in every one of their 6 combined conditions -- every 'claim' returned for either item has text=''.
confidence_interval: none -- raw counts at this n, not a rate estimate
failure_cases: n/a for the clamp itself (zero crashes this run); the pre-existing empty-text pattern remains the dominant real failure mode, most concentrated on items 0001, 0004, 0006, 0007
interpretation: The clamp fix works exactly as intended and no further: it eliminated the schema-crash failure mode (confirmed, 0/24 vs. EXP-009's 4/10 baseline) without touching, and without needing to touch, the separate empty-text-output failure mode, which remains real and unaffected. Most importantly, this directly re-tests and CONFIRMS rather than overturns the paper's original diagnosis for items 0006/0007: their zero-verifiable-claim result was never an artifact of the schema-crash bug this session fixed -- it is a genuine, still-present transcription-quality ceiling, exactly as research_paper/main.tex already reports. (An initial raw read of this run's claim COUNTS looked like a possible reversal of that finding; direct inspection of claim text content before drawing that conclusion showed every one of those counts was empty-text noise, not real recovered claims -- the correct, verified reading is reported here, not the initially-tempting one.)

hypothesis: Does extraction_confidence (the claim-extraction LLM's own self-reported MODEL_CONFIDENCE) correlate with claim groundedness -- specifically, whether the claim's source_quote is an independently, deterministically verifiable verbatim substring of the reel's real transcript/OCR/caption (app.pipeline.claim_extraction._infer_source_modalities, reused unchanged)? Named as a concrete next experiment in PHASE1_RESEARCH_NOTES.md, not yet run before this pass.
dataset: All 8 ingestible DEV-split (benchmark_v1) reels with real content (item-0003 excluded, never ingestible) -- VALIDATION-split items deliberately excluded from this exploratory/diagnostic measurement, reserved for Phase 3's later confirmatory use per RESEARCH_ROADMAP_V2.md
baseline: n/a -- first time this correlation has been measured
variant: production's real extract_claims() (full stack: quality-retry, Gemini escalation, dedup) run inside a rolled-back transaction per item, no persistence
model: llama3.2 (Ollama) primary, gemini-flash-latest fallback on quality-retry (fired on 1 of 8 items; a second item hit real GEMINI_API_KEY QUOTA_EXHAUSTED mid-run and correctly fell back to the raw llama3.2 result per the existing quota-aware fallback path, not a crash)
metrics: point-biserial correlation (extraction_confidence vs. binary grounded/ungrounded), computed via numpy.corrcoef
result: Correlation could NOT be computed: all 12 real claims returned across all 8 items had grounded=False (source_modalities empty) -- and specifically has_source_quote=False for every single one, including claims that look highly quotable on their face ('5,154 likes', '86 comments', exact OCR/caption numbers). Zero variance in the grounded dimension means no correlation exists to measure, not that the true correlation is zero.
confidence_interval: n/a -- undefined, not just wide, given zero variance in one variable
failure_cases: n/a for a crash sense (0 extraction failures across 8 items); the real failure is upstream of what this experiment could measure -- source_quote itself is essentially never populated in this real sample, a separate, prior gap from the one this experiment set out to check
interpretation: This is a real, disclosable null result, not a design failure of the experiment: the intended measurement (does confidence track groundedness) is blocked by a more basic, previously-undiagnosed gap -- claim_extraction's real-world source_quote fill rate looks very low even on claims that plausibly have a verbatim source (e.g. literal OCR/caption numbers). Two live hypotheses, not yet distinguished by this pass: (a) the prompt under-elicits source_quote relative to its own docstring instruction, or (b) many of these specific claims are genuinely legitimate paraphrases (e.g. 'This isn't democracy, it's vandalism' reads as commentary, not a quote) and the low rate is real and correct. Worth a dedicated follow-up (a source_quote fill-rate audit) before concluding either way -- not attempted this pass, logged as a candidate next step rather than guessed at.
